Introduction to Networks
• What is a Network? 
• A Collection of interconnected hosts (devices) that communicate 
and share 
resources.
• The uses of a network 
1.Simultaneous  Access  to  Data: Multiple  users  can  access  shared 
files and information at the same time, increasing efficiency and 
collaboration.
2.Resource Sharing: Networks enable devices to share resources like 
printers, file servers  (that manages and provides access to files), and 
internet connections.
3.Communication: Networks allow communication through various 
channels, such as email, video calls, and messaging.
4.Easier  Data  Backup: It  allows  for  simpler  and  more  effective  data 
backup and recovery processes.
5.Working  Remotely: Networks  provide  the  infrastructure  for  remote 
work, enabling users to connect to their organization's resources from 
any location.

Other Network Components
•Wireless Access Points (WAPs): Devices that allow wireless devices to connect to a wired network using Wi -Fi.
•Firewalls: Security devices (hardware or software) that monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic 
based on predetermined security rules, protecting networks from unauthorized access.
•Proxies: proxy is an intermediate server that sits between a client and another server. When you connect to a 
website or online service, your request can go through a proxy server first, which then forwards your request to 
the actual server. Proxies are used for security, filtering, caching. For example, a proxy can block access to certain 
websites, cache frequently accessed data to speed up browsing.
•Load Balancers: Devices or software used to distribute network or application traffic across multiple servers to 
ensure no single server is overwhelmed, improving availability and reliability.

Open System Interconnection (OSI) Protocol 
architecture
• The  OSI model  consists of  seven  separate  and distinct layers, each 
describing a particular set of functions and behaviours. 
• The OSI 7 layers model has clear characteristics at each layer. Basically, 
layers  7  through  4  deal  with  end-to-end  communications  between  data 
source  and  destinations,  while  layers  3  to  1  deal  with  communications 
between network devices. On the other hand, the seven layers of the OSI 
model can be divided into two groups: upper layers (layers 7, 6 & 5) and 
lower layers (layers 4, 3, 2, 1). The upper layers of the OSI model deal with 
application  issues  and  generally  are  implemented  only  in  software.  The 
highest  layer,  the  application  layer,  is  closest  to  the  end  user.  The  lower 
layers  of  the  OSI  model  handle  data  transport  issues.  The  physical  layer 
and  the  data  link  layer  are  implemented  in  hardware  and  software.  The 
lowest layer, the physical layer, is closest to the physical network medium 
(the wires, for example) and is responsible for placing data on the 
medium.

TCP/IP Model
• TCP/P architecture does not exactly follow the OSl model
• TCP/IP  architecture  omits  some  features  found  under  the  OS  model, 
combines  the  features  of  some  adjacent  OSI  layers  and  Splits  other 
layers apart. 
• The  4-layer  structure  of  TCP/IP  is  built  as  information  is  passed  down 
from applications to the physical network layer. When data is sent, each 
layer treats all of the information it receives from the upper layer as data, 
adds control information (header) to the front of that data and then pass it 
to the lower layer. When data is received, the opposite procedure takes 
place  as  each  layer  processes  and  removes  its  header  before  passing 
the data to the upper layer. Physical

2d4f37918597e476-2.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-2.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-2.text:
Introduction To Network Design
Network design is the process of planning, structuring, and 
documenting a computer network that will meet business and 
technical requirements. It involves making decisions about 
hardware, software, connectivity, topology, security, and 
scalability.
Network design is like drawing the blueprint of a building before 
construction.

2d4f37918597e476-4.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-4.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-4.text:
The Role of Network Design in IT
• Supports Business Goals
A bank needs 24/7 uptime, while a small office may accept occasional 
downtime.
 The network must be designed based on business priorities.
• Supports Applications
• Video conferencing requires low latency.
• File backups require high bandwidth.
• Security systems require reliable uptime.
• Reduces Costs
Good design avoids overbuying equipment while ensuring future growth.

2d4f37918597e476-5.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-5.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-5.text:
Network Design Goals
Scalability
The ability of the network to grow (more users, devices, applications, or sites) 
without performance degradation or a complete redesign.
 
• Current: 15,000 students, multiple campuses in Canterbury, Medway, and 
Tunbridge Wells.
• Future: Expansion to support 20% more students and new online learning 
services.
• Scalable design: Adding extra access points, VLANs, or cloud resources without 
replacing the entire network.

2d4f37918597e476-6.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-6.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-6.text:
Network Design Goals Cont’d
Availability
The ability of the network to deliver consistent, reliable service 
24/7, even when components fail.
• Online library system and student portals must be available day 
and night.
• Redundant internet connections ensure services keep running 
even if one ISP link fails.
• Failover routing keeps critical systems (e.g., Blackboard, Moodle, 
email) accessible during outages.

2d4f37918597e476-7.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-7.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-7.text:
Network Design Goals Cont’d
Security
Protecting the network from unauthorized access, attacks, and 
data breaches.
• Secure logins for staff and students (multi-factor 
authentication).
• Firewalls protect research databases and student records.
• Segmentation: student Wi-Fi is isolated from administrative 
systems.

2d4f37918597e476-8.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-8.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-8.text:
Network Design Goals Cont’d
Manageability
The ability of IT staff to efficiently monitor, configure, and troubleshoot 
the network.
• Centralized monitoring dashboards show traffic, device status, and 
potential issues.
• Automated alerts notify IT when a switch or Wi-Fi AP fails.
• Well-documented design helps new staff quickly understand and 
manage the network.

2d4f37918597e476-10.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-10.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-10.text:
Requirement Gathering
Understand what the network must achieve.
• Business requirements
• Growth plans (e.g., Christ Church University adding new 
campuses)
• Budget limits
• Compliance/regulation (GDPR, research data security)
• Technical requirements
• Applications (Blackboard, email, research databases)
• Bandwidth & latency targets
• Security levels (VPN, firewall policies)

2d4f37918597e476-11.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-11.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-11.text:
Site and Traffic Analysis
Study how the current network is used.
• Site survey
• Number of users per campus/building
• Wi-Fi coverage mapping
• Physical constraints (old buildings, wiring limitations)
• Traffic analysis
• Identify peak loads (e.g., start of term logins)
• Measure application usage (video streaming, online exams)
• Detect bottlenecks

2d4f37918597e476-12.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-12.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-12.text:
Conceptual, Logical, and Physical Design
(Three Layers of Design)
Conceptual Design
High-level view: “What services do we need?”
Internet access, secure VPN, online learning.
Logical Design
IP addressing schemes
VLANs, routing protocols
Security zones
Physical Design
Actual hardware: switches, routers, Wi-Fi access points
Cabling, racks, and data centers

2d4f37918597e476-14.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-14.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-14.text:
Validation & Documentation
Validation
• Simulate/test the design before going live
• Pilot installations in one building/campus
• Performance testing (latency, throughput, failover)

2d4f37918597e476-15.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-15.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-15.text:
Validation & Documentation
Documentation
• Network diagrams (logical + physical)
• Configuration details
• Maintenance procedures

2d4f37918597e476-16.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-16.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-16.text:
Deployment and Acceptance Testing
Deployment:
• Step-by-step introduction of devices & services
• Educating users (staff/students get login guides)
Acceptance testing:
• Final check with business stakeholders
• Confirm requirements are met (e.g., “Wi-Fi works for 1000 users 
simultaneously”)
• Handover to IT operations

2d4f37918597e476-17.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-17.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-17.text:
Tools for Design and Testing
• Packet Tracer: simulation of Cisco networks
• GNS3: emulate real routers, switches, firewalls
• NetFlow analysers: analyse traffic patterns
• Wireshark: packet capture for troubleshooting

2d4f37918597e476-20.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-20.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-20.text:
Network Design Approaches
Top-Down Approach:
Start with business and application requirements, then decide on 
technologies.
• Identify business goals
• Define application needs
• Translate into network requirements
• Select hardware/software to support them

2d4f37918597e476-21.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-21.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-21.text:
Network Design Approaches
Bottom-Up Approach
Start with available technologies and build upward to 
applications.
• Choose hardware/protocols first (switches, routers, Wi-Fi).
• Then adapt to meet applications and business needs.

2d4f37918597e476-22.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-22.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-22.text:
Network Design Approaches
Hybrid Approach
Combines Top-Down and Bottom-Up.
• Start with business/application goals.
• Consider available technology and budget limits.
• Adjust design accordingly.

2d4f37918597e476-31.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-31.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-31.text:
Core Layer
• Provides fast, reliable interconnection 
between distribution switches.
• Prioritizes speed, redundancy, and 
stability.
 
Example:
Fiber backbone links Canterbury, 
Medway, and Tunbridge Wells campuses.

2d4f37918597e476-32.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-32.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-32.text:
Distribution Layer
• Aggregates access layer traffic.
• Implements routing, filtering, VLANs, 
and security policies.
• Provides backup paths to the core.
Example:
Building-level distribution switches 
enforce VLAN separation (staff Wi-Fi vs 
student Wi-Fi).

2d4f37918597e476-33.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-33.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-33.text:
Access Layer
• Where end-users connect.
• Provides switch ports, Wi-Fi access points, and authentication.
 Example:
Students and staff connect laptops and phones via APs in lecture halls and libraries.

2d4f37918597e476-34.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-34.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-34.text:
Zero Trust Model in Network Design
A security model that assumes 
no user, device, or network is 
trusted by default, even if inside 
the network perimeter.
• Based on the principle:
 “Never trust, always verify.”

2d4f37918597e476-36.title: Lecture 2_Networking
2d4f37918597e476-36.label: Page
2d4f37918597e476-36.text:
Zero Trust in Practice
• Identity & Access Management (IAM): 
Multi-factor authentication (MFA).
• Network Segmentation: Divide traffic 
into smaller, controlled zones.
• Micro segmentation: Restrict access 
between workloads (e.g., labs vs admin).
• Continuous Monitoring: Use tools to 
analyse user/device behaviour.

TCP VS UDP
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is a connection-oriented protocol that ensures reliable and ordered delivery of data, complete with error checking and flow control mechanisms. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is a connectionless protocol favoured for its speed and efficiency, sacrificing reliability and order to reduce overhead and enhance performance in applications where occasional data loss is acceptable.

Examples: SSL/TLS (encryption), JPEG, MPEG.

Research is a Process

• It should follow a planned and structured process, e.g.
• Aim: identify effective teaching methods
• Research Question: does the rise in online teaching

How to Read a Paper
S. Keshav
David R. Cheriton School of Computer Science, University of Waterloo
Waterloo, ON, Canada
keshav@uwaterloo.ca
ABSTRACT
Researchers spend a great deal of time reading research pa-
pers. However, this skill is rarely taught, leading to much
wasted eﬀort. This article outlines a practical and eﬃcient
three-pass method for reading research papers. I also de-
scribe how to use this method to do a literature survey.
Categories and Subject Descriptors: A.1 [Introductory
and Survey]
General Terms: Documentation.
Keywords: Paper, Reading, Hints.
1. INTRODUCTION
Researchers must read papers for several reasons: to re-
view them for a conference or a class, to keep current in
their ﬁeld, or for a literature survey of a new ﬁeld. A typi-
cal researcher will likely spend hundreds of hours every yea r
reading papers.
Learning to eﬃciently read a paper is a critical but rarely
taught skill. Beginning graduate students, therefore, mus t
learn on their own using trial and error. Students waste
much eﬀort in the process and are frequently driven to frus-
tration.
For many years I have used a simple approach to eﬃciently
read papers. This paper describes the ‘three-pass’ approac h
and its use in doing a literature survey.
2. THE THREE-PASS APPROACH
The key idea is that you should read the paper in up to
three passes, instead of starting at the beginning and plow-
ing your way to the end. Each pass accomplishes speciﬁc
goals and builds upon the previous pass: The f irst pass
gives you a general idea about the paper. The second pass
lets you grasp the paper’s content, but not its details. The
third pass helps you understand the paper in depth.
2.1 The ﬁrst pass
The ﬁrst pass is a quick scan to get a bird’s-eye view of
the paper. You can also decide whether you need to do any
more passes. This pass should take about ﬁve to ten minutes
and consists of the following steps:
1. Carefully read the title, abstract, and introduction
2. Read the section and sub-section headings, but ignore
everything else
3. Read the conclusions
4. Glance over the references, mentally ticking oﬀ the
ones you’ve already read
At the end of the ﬁrst pass, you should be able to answer
the ﬁve Cs :
1. Category : What type of paper is this? A measure-
ment paper? An analysis of an existing system? A
description of a research prototype?
2. Context: Which other papers is it related to? Which
theoretical bases were used to analyze the problem?
3. Correctness : Do the assumptions appear to be valid?
4. Contributions: What are the paper’s main contribu-
tions?
5. Clarity : Is the paper well written?
Using this information, you may choose not to read fur-
ther. This could be because the paper doesn’t interest you,
or you don’t know enough about the area to understand the
paper, or that the authors make invalid assumptions. The
ﬁrst pass is adequate for papers that aren’t in your research
area, but may someday prove relevant.
Incidentally, when you write a paper, you can expect most
reviewers (and readers) to make only one pass over it. Take
care to choose coherent section and sub-section titles and
to write concise and comprehensive abstracts. If a reviewer
cannot understand the gist after one pass, the paper will
likely be rejected; if a reader cannot understand the high-
lights of the paper after ﬁve minutes, the paper will likely
never be read.
2.2 The second pass
In the second pass, read the paper with greater care, but
ignore details such as proofs. It helps to jot down the key
points, or to make comments in the margins, as you read.
1. Look carefully at the ﬁgures, diagrams and other illus-
trations in the paper. Pay special attention to graphs.
Are the axes properly labeled? Are results shown with
error bars, so that conclusions are statistically sig-
niﬁcant? Common mistakes like these will separate
rushed, shoddy work from the truly excellent.
2. Remember to mark relevant unread references for fur-
ther reading (this is a good way to learn more about
the background of the paper).
ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 83 Volume 37, Number 3, July 2007

e3d97831bc19b60a-2.title: keshav-how-to-readPaper
e3d97831bc19b60a-2.label: Page
e3d97831bc19b60a-2.text:
The second pass should take up to an hour. After this
pass, you should be able to grasp the content of the paper.
You should be able to summarize the main thrust of the pa-
per, with supporting evidence, to someone else. This level o f
detail is appropriate for a paper in which you are interested ,
but does not lie in your research speciality.
Sometimes you won’t understand a paper even at the end
of the second pass. This may be because the subject matter
is new to you, with unfamiliar terminology and acronyms.
Or the authors may use a proof or experimental technique
that you don’t understand, so that the bulk of the pa-
per is incomprehensible. The paper may be poorly written
with unsubstantiated assertions and numerous forward ref-
erences. Or it could just be that it’s late at night and you’re
tired. You can now choose to: (a) set the paper aside, hoping
you don’t need to understand the material to be successful
in your career, (b) return to the paper later, perhaps after
reading background material or (c) persevere and go on to
the third pass.
2.3 The third pass
To fully understand a paper, particularly if you are re-
viewer, requires a third pass. The key to the third pass
is to attempt to virtually re-implement the paper: that is,
making the same assumptions as the authors, re-create the
work. By comparing this re-creation with the actual paper,
you can easily identify not only a paper’s innovations, but
also its hidden failings and assumptions.
This pass requires great attention to detail. You should
identify and challenge every assumption in every statement .
Moreover, you should think about how you yourself would
present a particular idea. This comparison of the actual
with the virtual lends a sharp insight into the proof and
presentation techniques in the paper and you can very likely
add this to your repertoire of tools. During this pass, you
should also jot down ideas for future work.
This pass can take about four or ﬁve hours for beginners,
and about an hour for an experienced reader. At the end
of this pass, you should be able to reconstruct the entire
structure of the paper from memory, as well as be able to
identify its strong and weak points. In particular, you shou ld
be able to pinpoint implicit assumptions, missing citation s
to relevant work, and potential issues with experimental or
analytical techniques.
3. DOING A LITERATURE SURVEY
Paper reading skills are put to the test in doing a literature
survey. This will require you to read tens of papers, perhaps
in an unfamiliar ﬁeld. What papers should you read? Here
is how you can use the three-pass approach to help.
First, use an academic search engine such as Google Scholar
or CiteSeer and some well-chosen keywords to ﬁnd three to
ﬁve recent papers in the area. Do one pass on each pa-
per to get a sense of the work, then read their related work
sections. You will ﬁnd a thumbnail summary of the recent
work, and perhaps, if you are lucky, a pointer to a recent
survey paper. If you can ﬁnd such a survey, you are done.
Read the survey, congratulating yourself on your good luck.
Otherwise, in the second step, ﬁnd shared citations and
repeated author names in the bibliography. These are the
key papers and researchers in that area. Download the key
papers and set them aside. Then go to the websites of the
key researchers and see where they’ve published recently.
That will help you identify the top conferences in that ﬁeld
because the best researchers usually publish in the top con-
ferences.
The third step is to go to the website for these top con-
ferences and look through their recent proceedings. A quick
scan will usually identify recent high-quality related wor k.
These papers, along with the ones you set aside earlier, con-
stitute the ﬁrst version of your survey. Make two passes
through these papers. If they all cite a key paper that you
did not ﬁnd earlier, obtain and read it, iterating as neces-
sary.
4. EXPERIENCE
I’ve used this approach for the last 15 years to read con-
ference proceedings, write reviews, do background researc h,
and to quickly review papers before a discussion. This dis-
ciplined approach prevents me from drowning in the details
before getting a bird’s-eye-view. It allows me to estimate t he
amount of time required to review a set of papers. More-
over, I can adjust the depth of paper evaluation depending
on my needs and how much time I have.
5. RELATED WORK
If you are reading a paper to do a review, you should also
read Timothy Roscoe’s paper on “Writing reviews for sys-
tems conferences” [1]. If you’re planning to write a technic al
paper, you should refer both to Henning Schulzrinne’s com-
prehensive web site [2] and George Whitesides’s excellent
overview of the process [3].
6. A REQUEST
I would like to make this a living document, updating it
as I receive comments. Please take a moment to email me
any comments or suggestions for improvement. You can also
add comments at CCRo, the online edition of CCR [4].
7. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

dents: Hossein Falaki, Earl Oliver, and Sumair Ur Rahman.
My thanks to them. I also beneﬁted from Christophe Diot’s
perceptive comments and Nicole Keshav’s eagle-eyed copy-
editing.

Correct Use of Tenses
Use the present tense when you are writing about established knowledge.
• “Smoking increases the risk of coronary heart disease..” or Timeless facts.. “This 
paper presents the results of . . .” “Section 5.1 explains the difference between . . .”
Use the past tense when writing about a work reported or an experiment you carried 
out or a method you used in the past. 
• “In 2009, David published an alternative method to…” “Blood samples were 
collected..”
When writing about figures and tables use present tense. 
• “This figure shows that…”
Future tense indicates the study which will be conducted in the future; often used in 
research proposals, as proposals are written about the research that will be 
occurring in the near future.

Academic Style: Be Cautious
Avoid assertive language:  
• should, must or ought to 
• Always back up your point with evidence/argument 
Instead, be Cautious:
• probably, likely, seems, appears,  
• suggests, tend to..
• Don’t use absolute phrases such as “cats are cleverer than dogs”. Instead use 
more cautious phrases such as “cats tend to be cleverer than dogs”
• Avoid saying “obviously…” and “Of course…” as well “It can be seen…”

• Contractions (Shortened words, with missing letters from the original)
• Don’t ->  use “Do not..” 
Slang words (used in casual conversations) 
• no  stuff  or things
Abbreviations (Shortened forms of words and phrases)

3861d6a349aadf23-7.title: Week_2_ERModelling_Students
3861d6a349aadf23-7.label: Slide
3861d6a349aadf23-7.text:
Data Models
Conceptual Data Model
A conceptual data model provides a ‘’high-level’’ description of the data items with their characteristics and relationships.
We are going to look at Entity-Relationship Modelling, which is a type of conceptual data modelling.
Logical Data Model
A logical data model is a translation or mapping of the conceptual data model towards a specific implementation environment.
In our case, the implementation environment is PostgreSQL; a type of relational DBMS (or RDBMS for short).

3861d6a349aadf23-15.title: Week_2_ERModelling_Students
3861d6a349aadf23-15.label: Slide
3861d6a349aadf23-15.text:
Entity Type
An entity type is anything of significance about which information needs to be known or held, that is within our area of interest.
In an ER Model, entity types or depicted using a rectangle.
Note: 
A lot of people will use Entity Type and Entity interchangeably for the same thing; they mean Entity Type.
Definition-wise, an entity is a single occurrence of an entity type.
Example:
Entity = A single employee, a single product
Entity Type = A set (collection) of these that share characteristics. All employees, all products.

3861d6a349aadf23-18.title: Week_2_ERModelling_Students
3861d6a349aadf23-18.label: Slide
3861d6a349aadf23-18.text:
Naming of Entity Types
Entity Type names should be:
Unique
Meaningful
Singular, not plural
Conceptual, not physical
You will need to refer to this to check any entity type names you use from this point forward.

3861d6a349aadf23-19.title: Week_2_ERModelling_Students
3861d6a349aadf23-19.label: Slide
3861d6a349aadf23-19.text:
Attribute Types
Definition
An attribute type represents a property of an entity type.
For example, name and address are attribute types of the entity type Employee or Customer.
A single entity will have values for each of these attributes.
We tend to simply call attribute types attributes.
Advice
Some versions of ER models will show attribute types alongside the entity types.
For our model we will not be following this method.
We will be following the traditional, simpler, ER model that only shows entity types and their relations.
We will come back to Attribute Types and their importance later on when looking at Logical Data Modelling.

3861d6a349aadf23-23.title: Week_2_ERModelling_Students
3861d6a349aadf23-23.label: Slide
3861d6a349aadf23-23.text:
Cardinality Definitions
One-to-One
A row in table A can only have one matching row in table B, and vice-versa.
Not a common relationship type.
May be used for security purposes or to divide larger tables.
One-to-Many
The most common relationship type.
A row in table A can have many matching rows in table B, 
but
 a row in table B can only have one matching row in table A.
E.g. A Customer can make many Orders, but a single Order is associated with only one Customer.

3861d6a349aadf23-25.title: Week_2_ERModelling_Students
3861d6a349aadf23-25.label: Slide
3861d6a349aadf23-25.text:
Cardinality: Many-to-Many
Many-to-Many
These are not allowed in relational databases.
We must break (or decompose) many-to-many relationships down to two or more one-to-many relationships.
Another option is to introduce an intermediate table.
E.g. when many employees work on many projects, we can introduce an ‘Allocation’ table to match employees to projects.

3861d6a349aadf23-31.title: Week_2_ERModelling_Students
3861d6a349aadf23-31.label: Slide
3861d6a349aadf23-31.text:
Relationship Participation
Relationships will fall into the following categories:
Mandatory
Optional
Mandatory means that every instance in table 1 
must
 correspond to an instance in table 2.
Optional means that instances in table 1 
may
 have a corresponding instance in table 2.
Mandatory Relationship
Optional Relationship

3861d6a349aadf23-33.label: Slide
3861d6a349aadf23-33.text:
Summary
In using these techniques, we can deduce that:
ER Diagrams are created from a set of requirements intended to meet the data storage needs of a business process.
ER Diagrams provide a Conceptual Design, or Conceptual Model for data storage.
The Conceptual Model is used as the basis of a Logical Data Model.

The COUNT function is a useful tool and is especially useful when we have a lot of records. The
COUNT function does exactly what you would expect it to, it counts the results. The COUNT
function can retrieve results alone or be an additional result. We will look into how it can be
an additional result in a later workbook when we visit the GROUP BY function. For now, we’ll
look at COUNT in its simplest form.
SELECT COUNT("studentID")
FROM student
WHERE "homeCounty" = 'Greater Manchester';
The result is useful because it tells us how many records have a home county of Greater Manchester.
This removes the need for us to scroll through the records and manually count them, or look at
row numbers to see how many there are.

The IN function allows us to retrieve records for students with home counties County Durham,
York and Derbyshire. This is a quicker way than using the OR method.

62e72ad3fe27ba97-2.label: Page
62e72ad3fe27ba97-2.text:
1 Introduction
When querying tables, most of the time we are interested in information from many sources.
Relational Databases, by their very design, mean that they are built on relationships and when
querying them we need to make use of these relationships.
The main method of doing this is to use Joins. Are visually represented using Venn Diagrams
in this workbook.
There are four different types of joins which we will look through.
Note: Completion of workbooks are necessary to ensure that you are able to complete your
Logbook tasks.
2 Inner Join
The INNER JOIN function is the most common join you will use when querying tables. The join
will return all records that have matching records in each table. Visually we can see the INNER
JOIN as follows:
INNER JOINT able 1 T able 2
In the above illustration we can see that an INNER JOIN is all the records in Table 1 that have a
corresponding record in Table 2.
Type the following SQL into DataGrip carefully:
SELECT p."programmeName", s."schoolName"
FROM programme p
INNER JOIN school s
ON s."schoolId" = p."schoolFK";
There are a few things to note in this query. But ﬁrst we will look at the JOIN part.
This query is fetching results from two tables: programme and school. To retrieve appropriate
results, i.e. the correct school for each programme, we need to join the two tables. This is done
using the INNER JOIN command.
First, we select from one table, in this case programme, we then need toINNER JOIN the school
table, but we need to deﬁne on what we are joining the two tables. This is where the ON clause
comes in and it is here, we tell the query to join "schoolFK" to "schoolId".
Page 1 of 5

62e72ad3fe27ba97-3.title: Workbook3-Joins
62e72ad3fe27ba97-3.label: Page
62e72ad3fe27ba97-3.text:
Note: In the above examples, ‘p’ and ‘s’ are used as shorthand once declared within the SQL
query. The single letter when referencing tables in this way is called an ‘alias’.
2.1 Simplifying Inner Joins
The inner join is the most commonly used join when querying databases so it is only natural
that we can simplify it and thus, simplify our overall query. Type in the following query:
SELECT p."programmeName", s."schoolName"
FROM programme p, school s
WHERE p."schoolFK" = s."schoolId";
QUESTION:
/hand_rightWhat do you notice about the results?
We can simplify inner joins by replacing them with a WHERE clause, linking the matching
columns, which in this case are "schoolFK" and "schoolId". This is because we’re interested in
where Table 1 matches with Table 2.
2.2 Aliases
As previously noted, in each of the previous queries we have used aliases. The aliases used are
‘p’ for the programme table and ‘s’ for the school table.
We declare the aliases after we declare the table;FROM programme p and they provide a short-
cut to the queried table allowing us to call the table without continually typing the full table
name.
Aliases are a good practice to start when querying multiple tables; they simplify our query
and prevent the query from breaking. Sometimes multiple tables will have columns with the
same name, and this can cause issues when querying, aliases are a shortcut to prevent this from
happening.
Aliases are also handy if we want to use the same table twice in the same query, an example of
this is below:
SELECT r1."studentFK"
FROM registration r1
INNER JOIN registration r2 on r1."studentFK" = r2."studentFK"
AND r1."registrationId" != r2."registrationId";
This query joins an instance of registration to another, different, instance of registration and
joins based on StudentFK. However, we tell the query that we are only interested if the two
instances have different registrationId. In other words, this query is retrieving students who have
registered more than once.
3 Left Join
Left Joins are a form of an outer join. Outer joins ﬁnd records in tables that match the criteria
we given them, as well as rows that do not match the criteria we give them. The below diagram
is illustrates how this works in a left join.
Page 2 of 5

62e72ad3fe27ba97-4.label: Page
62e72ad3fe27ba97-4.text:
LEFT JOINT able 1 T able 2
If we have two tables, a left join selects all values in Table 1 and any values in Table 2 that meet
the criteria. In action, lets look at the sample tables below:
Number Square
2 4
3 9
4 16
Table 1
Number Cube
2 8
3 27
5 125
Table 2
Each table has a matching column, Number. If we do a LEFT JOIN with the two, we select all
values in T able 1, and any values from T able 2that match the criteria in T able 1(the criteria being
‘Number’), so we get:
Number Square Cube
2 4 8
3 9 27
4 16 NULL
Table 3
The record where ‘Number’ is 4 does not have a matching value in T able 2 and therefore the
value returns as NULL. Additionally, the row in T able2 where ‘Number’ is 5 is not included in
the result as it has no matching value in T able 1.
/warning_signFor the following example you will need to run the ClubCreation SQL script uploaded
alongside this Workbook on Blackboard.
The new table we have created registers some students to school clubs. However, not all stu-
dents have been registered, so let us see the Left Join in action. Type in the following SQL
carefully.
SELECT s."firstName", s."lastName", cr."clubFK"
FROM student s
LEFT JOIN "clubRegistration" cr ON s."studentId" = cr."studentFK";
Notice how the results are organised. At the top of the list are all the students who have a
matching record in the "clubRegistration" table, i.e. all the students who have signed up for a
club. Underneath are all the students who have no registration in the table so the values for
their registration is NULL.

62e72ad3fe27ba97-5.label: Page
62e72ad3fe27ba97-5.text:
In left join queries, the ﬁrst table, the one on the left hand side of the join, is the one declared at
the FROM part.
4 Right Join
By it’s name you should be able to guess what a RIGHT JOIN is, especially in comparison to
the LEFT JOIN. The right join works like a left join, but in the opposite direction, so selecting all
values from Table 2 and the values in Table 1 that match the criteria.
QUESTION:
/hand_rightIf we look at our previous sample tables, how would the RIGHT JOIN work on them?
/warning_signIn practice you would normally just use LEFT JOIN and swap the table order to achieve the
same result.
5 Full Outer Join
Sometimes we want to retrieve everything from two or more tables but join them wherever they
have matching criteria. In this case, we can use the FULL OUTER JOIN.
This type of join is one of the least commonly used, but it is important to be aware of. This can
be visually represented with the following diagram:
<—FULL OUTER JOIN—>
Both tables joined over a shared column, all data is included.
T able 1 T able 2
In a FULL OUTER JOIN we can join these two tables, as before, on the common column number,
but the join will return all values from table 1 and all values of table 2.
Number Square Cube
2 4 8
3 9 27
4 16 NULL
5 NULL 125
Table 4
After seeing left join and right join, you should notice that a full outer join is a combination of
the two. As we previously noted though, full outer joins are among the least likely to be used
in practice, but it is useful to be aware of.

Figure 1: Using CREATE SCHEMA in DBeaver.
When we look into the schema ‘library’, you will see there is nothing there so we need to make
our tables.
The ﬁrst table we are going to create is ‘student’.
But wait! We already have a table called student in our database, under the public schema. This
is why it was important to create our new schema ‘library’. Using library as a preﬁx we can
specify which student table we are referring to.
3.1 CREATE Syntax
The CREATE syntax uses several aspects that that enable an SQL script to create new data tables,
including:
• table_name: name of the table
• column#: column name
• datatype: the type of data we will allow in the column
• length: maximum length we allow
• nullability: if we do not allow nulls, we need to specify so
The following is an example of what the CREATE syntax looks like in practice:
CREATE TABLE table_name (
column1 datatype(length) nullability,
column2 datatype(length) nullability,
...
);
In addition to the above we can add other details, such as default values, unique, check condi-
tions and constraints.
With our syntax known, we can create our ﬁrst table, ‘student’.
As we identiﬁed before, we know that a student table already exists, so we need to preﬁx this
table with the assigned schema’s name, ‘library’. We, then get our ﬁrst line:
CREATE TABLE library.student (

a15ab12c0456e52a-4.label: Page
a15ab12c0456e52a-4.text:
3.2 CREATE Syntax: T able Columns
Next we want to deﬁne our ﬁrst column, and as per the diagram (SampleLibraryDB.png), it is
the Primary Key ’StudentId’.
Figure 2: The ’Student’ table from SampleLibraryDB.png.
So, our next line will look something like:
StudentId bigserial primary key,
As we are deﬁning this column as the primary key we don’t need to deﬁne it as NOT NULL.
Remember: The deﬁnition of a primary key means it can never be null, so the nullability is
already deﬁned.
The ‘bigserial’ data type is incredibly useful for when we create tables, it creates a sequence
when the table is created which automatically assigns the next integer value to the inserted
data, therefore ensuring consistent uniqueness across the primary key. The sequence only ever
goes forward, so no used number will ever be used again.
Now let us look at our next two columns which are similar to each other.
• FirstName
• LastName
Following our syntax we can deﬁne the next two rows:
FirstName varchar NOT NULL,
LastName varchar NOT NULL,
These are two simple columns, both alike each other. We don’t need to add lengths or defaults,
but we will require all records to have both values.
3.3 CREATE Syntax: Constraints
Our last attribute is a bit different as we have an additional detail on our model.
We have a data constraint which we should look to implement, we want to create a column for
‘Email’ with varchar and not null. This is the same as our ﬁrst name and last name ones, but we
also want to add the constraint “must contain ‘@’”.
Luckily for us, DDL provides us the CHECK command and we can use this to provide a data
check to anything being entered into this column and it looks like:

a15ab12c0456e52a-5.title: MCOMD2DEG____Workbook_4___DDL
a15ab12c0456e52a-5.label: Page
a15ab12c0456e52a-5.text:
Email varchar NOT NULL CHECK (Email LIKE ‘%@%’)
3.4 CREATE Syntax: Full CREATE Statement
Now, we have our last column, so we can bring them all together:
CREATE TABLE Student (
StudentId bigserial primary key,
FirstName varchar NOT NULL,
LastName varchar NOT NULL,
Email varchar NOT NULL CHECK (Email LIKE '%@%')
);
QUESTION:
/hand_rightHow would you create the table ‘Author’ from the Logical Data Model, using the CREATE
syntax?
/warning_signOnce you have an answer, run your SQL statement to create the ‘Author’ table in your data-
base.
When creating tables from a logical data model, it is easier to start with the tables that don’t
have foreign keys. If we try to create a table with a foreign key to a table we have yet to create,
the creation script will fail.
When designing your LDM, if you place the tables that do not have FKs on the outside edges
(so that those that do have FKs are in the centre), you can use the ‘work from the outside-in’
method, to create all of your tables.
3.5 CREATE Syntax: More on Constraints
We now have our ‘student’ and ‘author’ tables, so let’s create the ‘genre’ table. Like our ‘student’
table, there is a constraint, except this time it states that:
‘the value of Target should be one of ‘Young Child’, ‘Child’, ‘Teen’ or ‘Adult’ ”
So how do we create this? We will go attribute by attribute.
First we deﬁne our table:
CREATE TABLE library.genre (
genreId bigserial primary key,
Our ﬁrst attribute is similar to our studentId; we deﬁne it as big serial and as the primary key.
We can now deﬁne our next attribute, following the same conventions as explained for ‘First-
Name’ and ‘LastName’ in the student table.:
name varchar not null,
Again, there is nothing new about this attribute. Following on, our next attribute is slightly
different in that we are using a different data type; text.
Text is a deﬁned data type in PostgreSQL and is useful for attributes we know will hold a fair
bit of words, for example more than a sentence. So we get:
description text not null,

a15ab12c0456e52a-6.title: MCOMD2DEG____Workbook_4___DDL
a15ab12c0456e52a-6.label: Page
a15ab12c0456e52a-6.text:
Now we get to our last attribute and we can use a similar deﬁnition to our CHECK clause in
the student table. We need to CHECK that ‘Target’ is one of four values. For this, we use theIN
clause, as follows:
target varchar not null check (target in ('Young Child',
'Child', 'Teen', 'Adult'))
We have now deﬁned that the value entered in target must be one of the values, if it isn’t then
we will not accept it.
Note: When typing, please check the quotation around the values, they need to be single quo-
tation.
Putting this all together we get our third table deﬁnition, ‘genre’.
CREATE TABLE library.genre (
genreId bigserial primary key,
name varchar not null,
description text not null, target varchar not null check (
target in ('Young Child', 'Child', 'Teen', 'Adult'))
);
3.6 CREATE Syntax: Foreign Keys
Now, lets look at the ‘book’ table and how to deﬁne foreign keys when creating tables. There
are multiple ways, but we will use the CONSTRAINT command.
So, lets deﬁne our table:
CREATE TABLE library.book (
bookId bigserial primary key,
title varchar not null,
authorId int not null
According to our LDM, this is a foreign key, so lets deﬁne it before we move to our next attribute.
In this example we are using the same column name as the column it will refer to.
Reminder: In practice, naming conventions tend to be this method or our previous method of
using the sufﬁx FK. Generally, it is what you prefer as a user. Many companies have predeﬁned
conventions and will tell you which method they use.
Just remember, whichever method you use, make sure this is the method you use universally
across your database. Don’t have some tables using the FK sufﬁx and others using the Id sufﬁx.
Have a common convention across your creation.
The constraint comes after the nullability declaration, and before the comma to end the attribute
declaration. The syntax is:
CONSTRAINT fk_name REFERENCES referenced_table_name
Here, fk_name is a name that we declare. It must be unique, and the convention tend to be:
currentTableName_referencedTable_attributeName_fk
So, for our authorId foreign key, we would call it:
book_author_authorId_fk

What is 
Normalisation
?
Normalisation
 is a systematic approach of decomposing tables to eliminate data redundancy (duplication) and undesirable characteristics like Insertion, Update and Deletion Anomalies.
It is a multi-step process that puts data into tabular form and removes duplicated data from the relation tables.
Normalisation
 is used mainly for two purposes
Eliminating redundant data
Ensuring data dependencies make sense, i.e. data is logically stored.
Normalisation
 is essentially the successive decomposition of relations into ‘sub-relations’ that have certain ‘desirable properties’.
The decompositions 
must be reversable
, 
i.e. no information is lost.
